description: From pre-war activism to the 19th Amendment, flappers and the anti-flapper backlash in 1920s America.
content_html:
Women Before the First World War

In 1910, the lives of most American women were shaped by narrow social expectations. Married middle-class women were expected to manage the home and raise children. Working-class women often laboured in factories or domestic service but had no political voice. Women could not vote in federal elections. The suffrage movement had been campaigning since the 1840s, winning the vote in some western states, but federal suffrage remained elusive. Alongside the suffrage campaign, progressive women were active in social reform — campaigning against child labour, for better working conditions and for public health improvements.

The progressive era (roughly 1890 to 1920) saw women take on expanding public roles. Organisations such as the Women’s Christian Temperance Union gave women a platform for political action outside formal politics. Women like Jane Addams, founder of Hull House in Chicago, pioneered social work and urban reform. By 1910, women were already in the workforce in significant numbers — as teachers, nurses, secretaries and factory workers — though they were systematically paid less than men.

Key Fact

The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified on 18 August 1920, gave women the right to vote in all federal elections. It was a major political landmark, the result of seventy years of campaigning. However, it did not remove racial barriers: Black women in the South were systematically prevented from voting by the same Jim Crow laws and intimidation that blocked Black men.

The First World War and Women’s Work

The entry of the United States into the First World War in April 1917 opened new opportunities for women. With millions of men in uniform, women moved into jobs previously closed to them: working in munitions factories, on the railways and in offices. Approximately 11,000 women served in the US Navy in non-combat roles. This direct contribution to the war effort strengthened the argument that women deserved the vote. When the war ended, many women were pushed out of their wartime jobs as returning soldiers reclaimed them, but the experience of wartime work had permanently changed expectations.

The most iconic image of the 1920s woman was the flapper. Flappers were typically young, urban and middle-class. They wore short skirts (above the knee), cut their hair in a short “bob,” wore make-up, smoked cigarettes and drank cocktails in speakeasies. They danced the Charleston and the Black Bottom. They drove cars and attended college in increasing numbers. The flapper represented a deliberate rejection of the Victorian ideal of the modest, domestic “angel in the house.”

Jazz culture was central to the flapper lifestyle. The speakeasy, the cinema, the radio and the gramophone all gave young women new social spaces and new freedoms. Hollywood glamorised the flapper image through films starring actresses like Clara Bow, who was marketed as the “It Girl” and became one of the biggest stars of the decade. Fashion magazines spread the flapper look nationwide.

Key Fact

The flapper lifestyle represented real but limited change. It was largely restricted to young, urban, white, middle-class women. The majority of American women — working-class, rural, Black, immigrant — did not live like flappers. Most women still worked in low-paid domestic or clerical jobs and faced significant inequality in wages and career opportunities.

Margaret Sanger and Birth Control

One of the most controversial women of the decade was Margaret Sanger. Sanger had been campaigning for women’s access to birth control since the 1910s, arguing that women could not be truly free until they could control their own reproduction. She founded the American Birth Control League in 1921, which later became Planned Parenthood. Her work was controversial: contraception was still illegal in many states, and she was prosecuted multiple times. However, by the late 1920s, birth control clinics were operating in several major cities, and middle-class women were increasingly able to access contraception.

The changes in women’s lives during the 1920s provoked strong reactions. Religious fundamentalists and conservative commentators condemned flappers as immoral and dangerous to family life. Many states considered legislation to restrict short skirts or bobbed hair. The Ku Klux Klan explicitly campaigned to return women to their “proper place” in the home. Some women themselves were critical of the flapper, arguing that it prioritised fashion and pleasure over serious feminist goals.

By 1930, many of the freedoms associated with the flapper had retreated. The Great Depression made survival a priority; spending on fashion and entertainment collapsed; and conservative social attitudes reasserted themselves. Women were urged to give up jobs to men. The 1920s represented a partial and uneven change: significant for those who lived through it, but far from a complete revolution in women’s status.
exam_tip_html: When assessing whether the 1920s truly changed the role of women, examiners want you to weigh the genuine changes (the vote, the flapper, birth control access, more women in the workforce) against the significant limits (the Nineteenth Amendment excluded Black women in practice; flappers were a minority; wages still lower than men; conservative backlash). For 8-mark significance questions about the Nineteenth Amendment or the flapper, always address both the significance at the time and the limits — this is where top-band responses are won. For a 12-mark ‘How far do you agree’ question, the flapper as evidence of change but the continued exclusion of working-class and Black women as evidence of limits are your strongest analytical tools.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Nineteenth Amendment (ratified 18 August 1920) gave women the vote after seventy years of campaigning. However, Black women in the South were blocked from voting by Jim Crow laws, so the amendment’s effect was unequal in practice.
  • The flapper became the iconic image of the 1920s “new woman” — short skirts, bobbed hair, dancing and drinking in speakeasies. The reality was that this lifestyle was largely confined to young, urban, white, middle-class women; most American women remained in low-paid and unequal positions.
  • Margaret Sanger’s birth control campaign and the expansion of women in the workforce represented real if partial change. Conservative and religious opposition — including from the KKK — pushed back strongly. The Great Depression reversed many gains by 1930.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the flapper lifestyle in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Flappers wore short skirts above the knee and cut their hair in a short 'bob' [1], rejecting Victorian expectations of modest female dress and representing a deliberate challenge to traditional ideas about women's behaviour. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Nineteenth Amendment and its impact on women's lives.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature.
Feature 1: The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified on 18 August 1920, gave women the right to vote in all federal elections [1] — it was the result of over seventy years of campaigning by the suffrage movement. [1]
Feature 2: Despite the amendment, Black women in the South were prevented from voting by Jim Crow laws and intimidation [1] — the amendment therefore did not end racial inequality in voting rights. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the position of women changed during the First World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise cause with specific evidence and a clear explanatory chain.
Secure: Valid cause with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
From 1917, women moved into jobs previously reserved for men as millions of soldiers left for Europe — munitions factories, railways, offices. Approximately 11,000 women served in the US Navy in non-combat roles. This direct contribution strengthened the argument for the vote and permanently raised expectations, even though many women lost their wartime jobs when men returned.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the flapper lifestyle for American society in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence; clear causal link.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: provoked a conservative and religious backlash (KKK, fundamentalists, state legislation against short skirts); spread of consumer culture and fashion industry; challenged traditional family norms; contributed to the association between jazz, cinema and immorality in the eyes of conservatives; created a cultural divide between urban modernity and rural tradition.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was Margaret Sanger's birth control campaign for women in the United States in the 1920s?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance at the time and over time; precise evidence; sustained analysis.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may address only one dimension.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: birth control still illegal in many states; Sanger prosecuted multiple times; American Birth Control League founded 1921; middle-class urban women gaining access to contraception by late 1920s.
Over time: ABCL became Planned Parenthood; birth control eventually legalised nationally; Sanger's campaign established reproductive rights as a feminist issue; foundation of twentieth-century women's liberation movement.

practice_questions.text:
'The 1920s brought genuine equality for women in the United States.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement.
Agreement: Nineteenth Amendment gave women the vote in 1920; flapper lifestyle represented new social freedoms; more women in higher education and workforce; birth control access growing; Hollywood glamourised independent women.
Disagreement: Black women in South excluded from voting by Jim Crow; flapper lifestyle limited to young urban middle-class; wages remained lower than men's; majority of women in low-paid clerical or domestic work; conservative backlash strong; Great Depression reversed many gains after 1929.
Judgement: partial and unequal change — significant advances for some women but structural inequality persisted. 'Nation of contrasts' applies directly: the flapper existed alongside continued discrimination.

knowledge_checks.q: When was the Nineteenth Amendment, giving women the right to vote in federal elections, ratified?
What did Margaret Sanger found in 1921, which later became Planned Parenthood?
options: The National Association of Women Voters

knowledge_checks.q: The term _____ described the young urban women of the 1920s who wore short skirts, bobbed hair and rejected traditional expectations of female behaviour.
Although the Nineteenth Amendment gave women the vote, Black women in the South were still prevented from voting by _____ laws and intimidation.
Match each term or name to its description:
right: Activist who founded the American Birth Control League in 1921
Constitutional amendment ratified in 1920 giving women the vote
Young urban woman of the 1920s who wore short skirts and rejected traditional norms

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Nineteenth Amendment ratified, and what did it do?
flashcard_questions.a: 18 August 1920; it gave women the right to vote in all federal elections.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did many Black women in the South still not vote after the Nineteenth Amendment?
flashcard_questions.a: Jim Crow laws and intimidation prevented them from registering and voting.
A young urban woman who wore short skirts, bobbed hair, drank and danced, rejecting traditional female expectations.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Hollywood actress was marketed as the 'It Girl' and became one of the biggest flapper-era film stars?
Who was Margaret Sanger and what did she campaign for?
flashcard_questions.a: An American activist and nurse who campaigned for women's access to birth control.

flashcard_questions.q: What organisation did Margaret Sanger found in 1921?
flashcard_questions.a: The American Birth Control League (later Planned Parenthood).

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the First World War strengthen the case for women's suffrage?
flashcard_questions.a: Women moved into wartime factory, railway and office work while men were in uniform, proving their contribution to the national effort.

flashcard_questions.q: Which groups led the conservative backlash against the flapper lifestyle?
flashcard_questions.a: Religious fundamentalists, the Ku Klux Klan and social conservatives who condemned it as immoral.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did many of the freedoms associated with the flapper retreat after 1929?
flashcard_questions.a: The Great Depression made survival a priority; spending on fashion and entertainment collapsed and conservative social attitudes reasserted themselves.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the main limitation of the flapper as a symbol of women's liberation?
flashcard_questions.a: The lifestyle was largely restricted to young, urban, white, middle-class women — not working-class, rural or Black women.

glossary_terms.definition: The political campaign for women's right to vote, active in the United States from the 1840s until the passage of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.
A term for the young, urban woman of the 1920s who wore short skirts and bobbed hair, drank, smoked and danced in public, and rejected traditional expectations of female behaviour.
American activist and nurse (1879-1966) who campaigned for women's access to contraception and founded the organisation that later became Planned Parenthood.
The amendment to the US Constitution, ratified on 18 August 1920, which gave women the right to vote in all federal elections.
The organisation founded by Margaret Sanger in 1921 to campaign for women's access to contraception, later renamed Planned Parenthood.
The campaign, active in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, to restrict or ban the consumption of alcohol, in which many women's organisations played a leading role.
